I’ve been farming these 12 mu in Quzhou County for 37 years, and at 57 I still do most of the work myself with just my wife and me in the household. That means I have to be smart with labor. My mainstay is the wheat-maize double crop on 8 mu — it’s reliable and the market is always there. The other 4 mu I split between 2 mu of cotton and 2 mu of chili to spread my price risk and bring in some cash in late summer and autumn.

Right now it is mid-April, so my winter wheat is already in the ground and waking up from dormancy. This week I will top-dress it with urea and run the first irrigation to boost tillering. I will irrigate two more times before harvest in early June — at jointing and grain filling — and spray fungicide and insecticide twice. I use an improved wheat variety; after all these years I know which one performs best on my well-irrigated loam.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will no-till plant hybrid maize directly into the wheat stubble. With only two of us, there is no time to plough between crops. I will fertilize at sowing and side-dress at the big-flush stage, irrigate twice — jointing and flowering — and spray herbicide plus one insecticide pass. No-till also keeps the stubble to protect soil moisture.

For the 2 mu of cotton, I will rotary-till the plot in late April and sow a hybrid Bt cotton seed. Cotton needs careful water management, so I will irrigate three times — at sowing, flowering and boll formation — and spray pesticides three times for aphids and mites even though the Bt gene handles the bollworm. I expect around 350 kg of seed cotton per mu.

The remaining 2 mu goes to hybrid chili peppers. I will rotary-till and lay plastic mulch in late April, transplant seedlings, and keep them well-fed with extra potassium because chili needs it for fruit set. I will irrigate four times and spray for mites and viral diseases four times. If the weather cooperates I should get about 2,000 kg of fresh chili per mu.
